reviews.reason: Both members enforce the same server-side CertificateVerify selection constraint: an unoffered algorithm is permitted exactly when no valid chain can be produced without unsupported algorithms. The conditions are logical contrapositives with the same direction and no distinct error outcome.
Both members require HelloRetryRequest encoding and parsing to use the ServerHello wire structure; their conditions, direction, and prohibited distinct body layout are equivalent.
One member requires both encoding and decoding psk_ke as value 0, while the other is conditioned only on encoding. The first therefore contains a parser-direction check absent from the second.
Both members impose the same 0-through-32-octet bound on ClientHello.legacy_session_id for the serializer/parser, with the same prohibition on values longer than 32 octets.
Under the same condition that ClientHello contains supported_versions, both members require version negotiation to use that extension rather than legacy_version.

One member requires both encoding and parsing the ClientHello variant as OfferedPsks, while the other requires only encoding extension_data as OfferedPsks. Their implementation-check directions are not equivalent.
Both members require the NewSessionTicket EarlyDataIndication body to be encoded as uint32 max_early_data_size under the same message-type condition.

One member applies to connection-termination paths and the other to handshake-abort paths. Although both require alert X when an alert is sent, those are different protocol conditions and therefore different error-path checks.

Both members require a client Certificate sent in response to CertificateRequest to copy the request's certificate_request_context exactly, in the same response direction and with the same mismatch prohibition.
Both members require PskIdentity.obfuscated_ticket_age to be encoded as uint32; the condition and serialization direction are equivalent.

One member applies whenever sending a ServerHello, while the other applies only when the server negotiates TLS 1.3. The broader and narrower conditions are not equivalent even though both check for supported_versions.

Both members express the same server-side implication: a post-handshake CertificateRequest may be sent only if the client offered post_handshake_auth. The positive and negative conditions are logical contrapositives.
Both members require the server to send Certificate when its authentication uses certificates, with the same server-to-client direction and omission prohibition.

Both members check TLSCiphertext.opaque_type value 23, but one additionally requires it to be the first field and prohibits a different field order. That field-position check is absent from the other member.
One member checks only encoding AlertLevel.fatal as numeric value 2, while the other explicitly requires both encoding and decoding that mapping. Their directions are not equivalent.

All members include the TLSCiphertext legacy_record_version value check, but one additionally requires the field position after opaque_type and another covers parser behavior. The component therefore combines more than one atomic check.

All members require the server receiving or parsing a ClientHello to ignore an unrecognized extension rather than reject the message solely for that extension; the inbound condition and outcome are equivalent.
One member requires both encoding and parsing the ServerHello variant as uint16 selected_identity, while the other requires only encoding it. The parser-direction check is not shared.

The members do not use equivalent scopes: one is limited to the post-ServerHello flight, one broadly covers server requests for client authentication, and one requires the server itself to be authenticating with a certificate. These are not the same conditional ordering check.

One member applies to unspecified-alert connection termination and the other to unspecified-alert handshake abort. The required alert-selection rule matches, but the protocol error-path conditions do not.
Both members require TLS 1.3 elliptic-curve key shares to use the curve's single point format and prohibit point-format negotiation under equivalent conditions.
